description: Hello everyone! We are a group of students that decided to team up for this hackathon challenge ✨️
summary:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive fire-safety decision platform and automated ETL pipeline built on NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database. We unified and cleaned 1,292 real microgravity combustion experiments from 16 tables across 15 ISS and Cygnus investigations (BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE I-III, FLEX, FLEX-2, SAME, SAME-R, and ACME) without fabricating missing values.
To address the challenge, our app organizes scattered spreadsheets into four safety pillars—Prevention, Detection, Suppression, and Fundamental physics—and provides three core tools: a Condition Map that overlays NASA's planned Moon-base atmosphere (>=30% O2, ~70.3 kPa) onto existing tests, a Nearest-Neighbor "What-If" Explorer that retrieves the closest historical experiments for any cabin scenario, and a grounded Gemini AI assistant where every cited [Test-ID] opens the official NASA record and DOI.
This is critical because microgravity flames behave as ventilation-driven spheres, and oxygen-rich lunar habitats make materials far more flammable. Our analysis revealed a major lunar safety gap—zero solid-material tests in PSI reach >=30% O2—helping engineers design safer habitats for the ISS, Moon, and Mars while supporting Earth spin-offs in smoke detection and clean fire suppression.
details:
What It Does & How It Works
Flame in Freefall is an end-to-end fire-safety decision platform and automated ETL pipeline built on NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. Spacecraft combustion data is currently scattered across dozens of raw, inconsistently formatted tables. Our platform automatically downloads, cleans, and unifies 1,292 real microgravity experiments from 16 experimental tables across 15 ISS and Cygnus investigations into a single interactive dashboard:

  • Overview & Explorer: Categorizes all 1,292 tests into four fire-safety pillars—Prevention (BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE I–III, ACME BRE), Detection (SAME, SAME-R), Suppression (FLEX, FLEX-2), and Fundamental/Partial-g Analogue physics (ACME CFI-G, Flame Design, CLD, s-Flame, E-FIELD). Engineers can filter by investigation, material, oxygen concentration, pressure, and airflow, and click any row to inspect the full NASA record and official DOI.
  • Condition Map: Plots all tests across oxygen-vs-airflow and oxygen-vs-pressure space, overlaying NASA’s planned Moon-base atmosphere (>=30% O2 at ~70.3 kPa / 10.2 psi) to expose testing blind spots.
  • Data-Driven "What-If" Explorer: Uses normalized Euclidean nearest-neighbor similarity across O2, pressure, and airflow to retrieve the closest historical NASA experiments for a user-defined cabin scenario, reporting how often flames established themselves, average CO spikes, and explicit dataset limitations.
  • Grounded AI Assistant (Ask AI): A retrieval-augmented Gemini 3.5 Flash assistant that answers engineering questions strictly using the 1,292 PSI records, embedding clickable [Test-ID] citations that open the original experiment drawer.

Benefits & Intended Impact

In microgravity, hot gases do not rise; flames form spheres driven by diffusion and cabin ventilation. Furthermore, planned lunar exploration atmospheres (>=30% O2 at reduced pressure) make materials significantly more flammable than on Earth. By unifying NASA’s data, our project revealed a critical safety gap: 0 solid-material tests in PSI reach >=30% O2 (BASS-II and SAFFIRE stop around 22.2% O2), whereas liquid droplet tests like [FLEX-20] (34% O2, ~72 kPa) burned to completion. Our platform also highlights that reducing ventilation airflow extinguished 19 PMMA tests in BASS-II, that 128 of 173 CO2/Helium-diluted FLEX tests ended in extinction, and that 4 of 4 Silicone samples in SAFFIRE-II self-extinguished in 0g despite burning in 1g. This helps mission planners select safer cabin materials for the ISS, Moon, and Mars, while supporting Earth spin-offs such as fine-water-mist extinguishers and multi-criteria smoke detectors.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • * Backend & ETL: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pandas, and NumPy, plus an automated downloader (requests) interfacing with the NASA PSI API.
  • * Frontend & Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript, and Plotly.js (scattergl, horizontal bar charts, and risk gauges).
  • * AI Integration: Google Gemini API (gemini-3.5-flash / gemini-2.5-flash via google-genai) with custom context-retrieval scoring.

Creativity & Factors Considered

Our team prioritized scientific integrity and zero fabricated data. Instead of training a black-box model that guesses missing values, we kept unreported NASA fields transparent (n/r), flagged cabin-pressure assumptions, and built automated parsers to fix raw spreadsheet errors (such as correcting 3400% and 2100% formatting typos in ACME BRE to 34% and 21% O2, and converting mmHg, bar, and atm to kPa). Finally, we designed the architecture to seamlessly ingest partial-gravity combustion data from NASA’s upcoming LUCI and FM2 lunar investigations.
